author: Miyamoto Musashi
biz: Musashi warns against a favourite weapon, because a preference dressed as a principle gets you killed. Your leads come from Google, Bing, Facebook and search, and it is easy to keep loving whichever worked last quarter. This week, rank each source not by cost per lead but by cost per completed, funded case, and sit a quality number beside it: complaint rate and the proportion of cases where a vulnerability was identified and properly handled. Measure both monthly. If a cheap source produces poor outcomes for customers, that is a cost, and Consumer Duty treats it as one.

Musashi tells you to look at the fight from the other man's position. For Debt Support Direct, that means hearing your own call the way a frightened client hears it. This week, review five recent calls and score one thing only: could the client afterwards restate in their own words that you are a broker and not a lender, that nothing is guaranteed, what any fee is, and what their alternatives are. Measure the percentage who could. Anything under full marks is a script problem to fix, not a training excuse.

b: He was born around 1584, and almost everything after that sentence is argued over. In the book he wrote at the very end of his life he said he came from Harima province. The historian Kamiko Tadashi looked at the village Musashi named, a place called Miyamoto, and placed it just over the border in Mimasaka. One of the earliest biographies, the Niten Ki, gives the year as 1583 instead. One of the most famous men in Japanese history, and we cannot be sure of his birthday or his county.

What is firmer is the house he grew up in. His father was Shinmen Munisai, a fighting man who taught the sword and was a recognised master of the jitte, a short iron bar with a hook on the side, used to catch and break an opponent's blade. Munisai taught his son to use it. So the boy's first lessons were not in the romance of the sword. They were in the awkward business of taking a weapon away from a man trying to kill you.

In 1596, aged about thirteen, he walked out to meet a travelling swordsman named Arima Kihei, of the Kashima Shinto school, and beat him. The only reason we know is that Musashi mentioned it himself, in one flat sentence, nearly fifty years later. No account of what was said, no crowd, no record of what the boy felt. The story has been embroidered a thousand times since. The record is one line.

It matters that the book begins where the boy began, because the first of its five scrolls does not begin with swords. It begins with a carpenter, who knows his timber, keeps his tools sharp, and knows which of his men can be trusted with delicate work and which should carry. Strategy, Musashi says, is a trade like that. Not a philosophy you agree with. A trade you are competent at or you are not.

b: At about sixteen he fought Tadashima Akiyama, from Tajima province, and won again. Then he disappears into the roads of a country finishing a civil war, and the record thins to almost nothing.

In October 1600 the great battle of Sekigahara settled who would rule Japan for the next two and a half centuries. Musashi is traditionally placed there, and for a long time he was assumed to have fought on the losing western side, because his family were connected to the Ukita. More recent work has pushed the other way. Records of the Kuroda house list his father among vassals on the winning eastern side. Another scholar, Kengo Tominaga, suggested that Musashi was not at Sekigahara at all but was fighting in Kyushu, at a smaller action called Ishigakihara. The honest summary is that nobody knows whether he was there, and if he was, which way he faced.

In the Book of Five Rings he writes that between the ages of thirteen and twenty nine he fought more than sixty contests and was never beaten. No independent document confirms that tally. It is his own account of his own life, given as a credential at the start of a manual.

This is the first thing the book teaches that nobody expects. He spends the opening pages telling you that he won constantly in his twenties and then says, plainly, that he did not understand why. He puts the wins down to natural ability, luck, and opponents who were simply worse, and says it was only around the age of fifty that he began to grasp what he had actually been doing. Thirty years of winning before the understanding arrived. That is a very unusual thing for a famous man to put in writing.

b: Around 1604, in his early twenties, he came to Kyoto, then the centre of sword teaching in Japan, and picked a fight with an institution. The Yoshioka were a fencing family with a school and a reputation. He fought them three times. First Seijuro, on Rendai moor west of the city. Then Denshichiro, outside the city. Then the youngest, Matashichiro, by a pine tree at Ichijoji, where the family are said to have brought a crowd of followers.

All of this comes from biographies written long after he died, and the versions do not agree. Even his age in that year differs between accounts. Be careful with the detail. The shape, that a young provincial took on an established city school and came away with his reputation made, is as much as the record safely gives.

In the same period he is said to have gone to the Kofuku temple in Nara and beaten Okuzoin Doei, a spear fighter of the Hozoin school. Beating a spearman with a sword means closing a distance designed to be uncloseable. If true, it tells you what he was practising.

It is the Ichijoji fight, the one against a crowd, that leaves its mark on the book. When Musashi writes about facing many men at once, his advice is cold and spatial. Do not let them surround you. Drive them so that they are strung out in a line rather than spread in a ring, go hard at the leading edge, keep moving so that the ones behind are always arriving late. It is the only part of the book where he really recommends the two swords he is famous for, and he recommends them there for a specific reason, which is that a man facing a crowd must cover two directions at once.
ch.cap: Dawn by the pine at Ichijoji, armed men among the trees

b: On the thirteenth of April 1612, on a small island near Shimonoseki, Musashi fought the most famous duel in Japanese history, against a swordsman called Sasaki Kojiro, who favoured a very long blade.

The telling goes like this. Musashi arrived late on purpose, leaving Kojiro on the beach growing angrier. On the boat over he took a spare oar and carved it into a rough wooden sword, longer than Kojiro's steel. They met once. Musashi brought the oar down on his head and that was the end of it.

Every vivid part of that account comes from later retellings rather than from a document written at the time, and historians disagree about nearly all of it, including who Kojiro actually was and how old he was. Some accounts have him as a young prodigy, others as an older master. Treat it as the best known story about Musashi rather than as a reliable report of an afternoon.

What survives the doubt is the idea that made the story worth telling, because that idea is all over the book. Musashi has no romance about equipment. He tells you not to have a favourite weapon. Favouring one thing, he says, is as bad as not knowing it at all. Use the long sword in open ground and the short one in a confined space, and if what you have to hand is a piece of wood then the only question is what length of wood this particular man requires. The fourth scroll, called Wind, is given over entirely to attacking other schools, and his sharpest contempt is for the ones that had made a doctrine out of a preference, the long sword men, the short sword men, the ones with secret teachings for favoured pupils. A preference dressed up as a principle was how a fighter got himself killed.
ch.cap: Carving a wooden sword from an oar on the crossing

b: In the winter of 1614 and again in the summer of 1615 the Tokugawa finished off the last organised opposition in Japan at Osaka castle. Musashi was there, on the Tokugawa side, in the force of Mizuno Katsunari. Clan records say he carried his commander's banner and guarded the commander's son. No feat of arms by him is documented.
So the greatest duellist of the age went to the largest battle of the age and the sources have nothing to say about him. A duel is a stage. A siege is a job.

The third scroll of the book, called Fire, is where he makes the claim that holds the whole thing together. The principles do not change with the number of people. One man against ten uses the same rules as a thousand against ten thousand. You take the high ground. You put the sun or the wind behind you and in your enemy's face. You push him onto ground he cannot use, a slope, a marsh, a narrow place. You arrive in a state that does not need to settle, and you do not let him settle. You find the point where his rhythm is about to break and you go there.

That claim is why a seventeenth century fencing manual ended up on the shelves of people who will never hold a sword. A one on one contest is not a special case. It is the same shape of problem as a campaign, seen close up, and if you can see the shape in one you can see it in the other.
ch.cap: A banner carried forward below the walls of Osaka

b: After Osaka the duelling largely stops, and the next twenty years are the part of his life almost nobody tells. He took service with the Ogasawara in Harima as a supervisor of construction, laying out ground, organising labour, building. The master carpenter of the first scroll was not a metaphor reached for from a distance. He had done the job.

He adopted sons. One, Mikinosuke, entered service with Mizuno Katsunari and in 1626 killed himself on the death of his lord, following the old practice of junshi. Another, Iori, went with Musashi to Kokura in 1634 as guests of the Ogasawara, where Musashi fought a lance specialist named Takada Matabei and won.

And in these years he became a painter. Not a swordsman who dabbled. His surviving ink paintings are held as serious works of art. The best known is a shrike perched on a withered branch. It is almost nothing. One bare vertical branch, one small hunting bird at the top of it, a great deal of empty paper, a few strokes of the brush loaded with ink so dry it breaks as it drags. The bird is alert and the branch is dead and that is the entire painting.

That is the aesthetic of his book as well. The Book of Five Rings is very short and very plain. The second scroll, Water, works through the body in that same dry manner. Hold your head level, neither drooping nor pushed up. Keep your everyday bearing when you fight and your fighting bearing when you go about your day, so there is no gear change and nothing to betray you. Widen the eyes so that you take in the whole field and stop staring at the thing in front of you, because the sword you can see is rarely the one that kills you.
ch.cap: One bird, one branch, nothing else on the paper

b: Between December 1637 and April 1638 the Tokugawa put down a rising at Shimabara, a desperate affair of starving peasants and masterless men behind the walls of an old castle. Musashi, by then in his fifties, was attached to the besieging force, and this is the one episode where documents place him at a battle rather than tradition placing him there. A journal recording his old commander Mizuno Katsunari has him walking into the camp and announcing that he knew the Osaka system of warfare well. There is also a story that he was knocked off his horse by a stone thrown from the walls. That one is thinly sourced and should be held loosely.

In 1640 the Hosokawa took him on properly at Kumamoto. The Niten Ki says he was given seventeen retainers, a stipend of three hundred koku of rice, a rank in the household and a residence on the grounds of the old Chiba castle. After fifty years of being nobody's man he had a position and pupils.

Pupils are what forced the book into existence. In the second month of 1641 he wrote a document for his lord called the Thirty Five Instructions on Strategy, the skeleton the Book of Five Rings would later be built on. Having to teach made him say out loud what he had been doing with his hands for half a century.

The heart of what he taught is a thing rendered in English as no attitude. He lists the five ways of holding a sword, upper, middle, lower, right and left, says the middle one is the commander and the others the troops, and then says the best position is the one that is not a position. A stance announces an intention. A man who has settled into a posture has told you what he intends and limited what he can still do. Musashi wants you standing in a way that is simply ready, committing to nothing, so that the cut is decided by what the other man does and not by what you had planned.
ch.cap: Winter siege lines at Shimabara, a camp at first light

b: In 1643, at about sixty, he left the town for a cave called Reigando in the hills outside Kumamoto, and began writing. He finished in the second month of 1645. The book is organised around the five elements of Buddhist tradition and is barely the length of a long pamphlet.

The first scroll, Earth, is the ground plan. Strategy is a craft, the carpenter is the model, and he sets out rules for the student that are almost comically unmystical. Think about what is right. Learn the Way in practice, not in talk. Know something of every trade, not only your own. Understand gain and loss in ordinary matters. Notice small things. Perceive what cannot be seen. Do not do anything useless.

The second scroll, Water, is the individual, the body, the eyes, the grip, timing, the named cuts. The third, Fire, is the fight itself, and it holds his three ways of taking the lead, the most portable idea in the book. You can forestall by going first and imposing your own thing. You can forestall by letting him come and turning his attack as it arrives. Or you can forestall by setting out at the same moment as him and breaking his movement inside his own attempt. Attack, receive, or accompany. Whichever you choose, the one thing you must never do is simply respond, because then the fight belongs to him.

The fourth scroll, Wind, is the demolition of the other schools. The fifth, Void, is three paragraphs long and is about what you cannot see. Musashi means nothing mystical by emptiness. He means the state of a man who has done the work so thoroughly that there is no gap left between seeing and doing, and therefore nothing in his mind to be read, exploited or disturbed. He says that in that emptiness there is good and no evil, and then he stops writing.
ch.cap: Writing the five scrolls by candlelight at Reigando

b: He gave the manuscript away before he died. The accounts differ in the usual irritating way, one saying he handed it to his pupil Terao Magonojo seven days before the end, another that it went to Magonojo's younger brother on the twelfth day of the fifth month.

At about the same time he wrote a stranger document, the Dokkodo, the way of walking alone. Twenty one short lines of renunciation, written by a man with days left. He gives up resentment, desire for possessions, preference in food, any wish for a comfortable house, regret, complaint. One line is usually rendered as respecting the gods and the Buddha without counting on their help.

He died around the thirteenth of June 1645, aged about sixty one, though one early biography says sixty two. A later tradition says a disease of the chest. Even the room is disputed. The Niten Ki has him dying in the cave, the earlier Bukoden says a local lord persuaded him back to the old castle grounds at Kumamoto. He is said to have gone seated, sword in his left hand, cane in his right. A tomb was set up for him on Mount Iwato.

One last honest note. Most of what the world thinks it knows about Musashi comes from a novel. Eiji Yoshikawa serialised Musashi in a Japanese newspaper in the nineteen thirties and published it in volumes from 1936 to 1939. It is a magnificent book and it is fiction. The monk who locks the young hothead in a room full of books, the patient girl waiting, the moral education of a wild boy into a sage, all of that is Yoshikawa. The man in the record is harder to love and more interesting. A provincial fighter with a disputed birthplace who won for thirty years without understanding why, spent twenty quiet years laying out building sites and painting birds, took a job at nearly sixty, then went up a hill to write the trade down in plain language because somebody had finally asked him to teach it.

connects: Sun Tzu and Musashi both treat strategy as a practical craft of position, timing and rhythm rather than a code of honour, and both insist the small contest and the large one obey the same rules.
Robert Greene's account of the long, unglamorous apprenticeship is almost exactly Musashi's own story, thirty years of doing the thing in his hands before he could say what he was doing.
Musashi's no attitude and Csikszentmihalyi's flow describe the same disappearance of self-conscious effort, the state in which seeing and acting stop being two separate steps.
note: Dates and names follow the mainstream modern accounts of Musashi's life, which rest on early biographies such as the Niten Ki, the Bukoden and the Hyoho senshi denki, all written after his death and often in disagreement. His birth year is given as 1583 or 1584 and his birthplace is disputed between Harima and Mimasaka. Whether he fought at Sekigahara in 1600, and on which side, is actively debated, and the celebrated Ganryujima duel of 1612 survives only in later retellings. The Shimabara campaign of 1637 to 1638 is the one engagement documents place him at. The famous scenes with the monk Takuan and the girl Otsu are inventions of Eiji Yoshikawa's novel, not history.
recall: What happened on the island off Shimonoseki on 13 April 1612, and what should you be careful about in the story?

Musashi fought Sasaki Kojiro and killed him with a wooden sword he is said to have carved from a boat oar on the crossing. Every vivid detail of that account comes from much later retellings rather than contemporary documents, and historians disagree even about who Kojiro was and how old he was.
What are the five scrolls of the Book of Five Rings, and what does each one cover?

Earth sets out strategy as a craft, using the master carpenter as the model. Water covers the individual body, eyes, grip and timing. Fire covers the fight itself and taking the lead. Wind attacks the other schools. Void, only a few paragraphs long, covers acting without any gap between seeing and doing.
What are Musashi's three ways of taking the lead?

You can go first and impose your own action. You can let the attack come and turn it as it arrives. Or you can set out at the same moment and break the movement inside the opponent's own attempt. His point is that you must never merely respond, because then the contest belongs to the other man.
What did Musashi write in the second month of 1641, for whom, and why does it matter?

He wrote the Thirty Five Instructions on Strategy for his lord Hosokawa Tadatoshi at Kumamoto. It is the skeleton the Book of Five Rings was later built on, and it exists because having pupils finally forced him to put fifty years of practice into words.
Which trade does Musashi use as his model for strategy, and why is the choice not merely decorative?

He uses the master carpenter, who knows his timber, keeps his tools sharp and knows which of his men to trust with fine work. The choice is not decorative because Musashi spent roughly twenty years as a supervisor of construction in Harima, so he was describing a job he had actually done.
recap: Here is the story in miniature. A boy is born somewhere in western Japan around 1584, into a house where his father teaches not the romance of the sword but the awkward trade of taking a weapon off a man. At about thirteen he walks out and beats a travelling swordsman, and we only know because he mentions it in one flat line half a century later. He vanishes into the roads of a country finishing a civil war. Whether he fought at Sekigahara, and on which side, historians still argue. In his early twenties he takes on an entire Kyoto fencing family in three separate fights and makes his name. In 1612, on an island near Shimonoseki, he kills Sasaki Kojiro with a wooden sword he is said to have carved from a boat oar on the way over, which is the most famous story about him and the least verifiable. Then the great siege of Osaka, where the sources have nothing to say about him at all, and twenty quiet years supervising building sites, adopting sons, and painting a shrike on a withered branch with almost nothing else on the paper. At nearly sixty the Hosokawa finally give him a household and pupils, and pupils force him to explain himself. In 1643 he goes up to a cave called Reigando and writes the Book of Five Rings, finishing early in 1645, and dies in June of that year, aged about sixty one. Five ideas to keep. Strategy is a trade like carpentry, learned in the hands, not a philosophy you agree with. Never have a favourite weapon, because a preference dressed up as a principle will get you killed. Never settle into a stance, because a stance tells the other man what you intend and limits what you can still do. There are three ways to take the lead, going first, turning what comes, or moving at the very same moment, and the one thing you must not do is merely respond. And the rules do not change with scale, because one man against ten is the same shape of problem as a thousand against ten thousand. One line to remember. He won for thirty years before he understood why, and the book exists because somebody finally asked him to teach.
stories: In April 1612 Musashi was rowed out to a small island near Shimonoseki to fight Sasaki Kojiro, a man famous for an unusually long blade. He turned up late on purpose, leaving Kojiro to stew on the beach, and on the crossing he picked up a spare oar and whittled it into a rough wooden sword slightly longer than his opponent's steel. They met once. One blow from the oar ended it. The turn is that he had quietly solved the problem on the boat, before either of them drew. The point is that he refused to accept his opponent's terms, including the reach of his weapon.
The bird on the dead branch

For twenty years after the great siege of Osaka, Japan's most formidable duellist mostly laid out building sites and painted. His best known picture is a shrike perched near the top of a bare, withered branch, surrounded by empty paper, done in strokes so dry the ink breaks as it drags. No decoration, no background, nothing pretty. Art historians rate it seriously. The turn is that the swordsman turns out to be a real painter. The point is that his whole method was the removal of everything that was not necessary.

A few days before he died in 1645, Musashi wrote the Dokkodo, the way of walking alone. It is twenty one short lines, and every one of them gives something up. No resentment. No desire for possessions. No preference about food. No wish for a comfortable house. No regret for anything done. One line respects the gods and the Buddha without counting on their help. He is said to have died seated, sword in his left hand, cane in his right. The point is that he had stripped his life to the practice and did not pretend it had been otherwise.
take: Winning is not the same as knowing why you won

Musashi won constantly in his twenties and said he only understood it near fifty. Audit your wins as hard as your losses, or you will keep repeating something that worked for a reason you have not identified.
Do not have a favourite weapon
A preference you have dressed up as a principle will get you killed. Keep every tool live and let the situation pick, not your habit.
The most useful position is the one that commits to nothing. Stay genuinely ready rather than pre-committed, so the other party's move decides yours.
Go first, receive and turn, or move at the same instant and break them inside their own attempt. What you must never do is merely respond, because then the contest is theirs.
Scale does not change the shape
One against ten follows the same rules as a thousand against ten thousand. Solve the small version properly and you have the big one.
Learn the trade in your hands
He compares strategy to carpentry because he had actually supervised building sites. Theory you have never executed is not knowledge, it is vocabulary.
He painted, he built, he fought. His rule was to understand the Ways of all professions, because the pattern you need is usually already solved somewhere else.
He tells you to perceive the whole field rather than stare at the nearest threat. The sword you are watching is rarely the one that reaches you.
title: The Man Who Won for Thirty Years Before He Understood Why
wiifm: You will meet a man who won more than sixty fights and then admitted in writing that he had no idea how. What he worked out in the thirty years afterwards is a set of tools you can use on Monday: why having a favourite method is as dangerous as having no method, why a settled posture tells your opponent everything, and the three ways of taking the lead in any contest, whether you go first, let it come, or move at the same moment. You will also get a clear line between the real Musashi and the novel almost everybody has mistaken for him.
words: Travelling from place to place rather than settled in one home or post.
Musashi was an itinerant swordsman for decades before the Hosokawa finally gave him a household at Kumamoto in 1640.
Widely repeated but of doubtful authenticity.
The carved oar at Ganryujima is the most famous thing about him and is almost certainly apocryphal in its details.
The Book of Five Rings is laconic to the point of bluntness, and his ink painting of a shrike on a dead branch has the same quality.
To act in advance so as to prevent or pre-empt what somebody else is about to do.
The third scroll gives three ways to forestall an opponent, by attacking first, by turning his attack, or by moving at the same instant as him.
A biography that treats its subject as a saint rather than as a person.
The early lives of Musashi are closer to hagiography than to history, which is why so many of the best stories cannot be verified.
